Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

herself pronoun

also by herself, she herself

classical

Verg. G. 1.389: sōla in siccā sēcum spatiātur harēnā

suī, sibi, sē (sēsē)

pronoun, reflexive: genitive suī, dative sibi, accusative and ablative sē; the same for every gender and number

herself (as object), referring to the subject

The same reflexive as for “himself”: sē does not change for a woman. “With herself, by herself” is sēcum, often with sōla.

Other words

  • ipsa — herself (for emphasis: she herself, of her own accord)

    pronoun, intensive: feminine of ipse · classical · Mart. 13.23.2: ipsa merum sēcum portat et ipsa salem; Phaedr. 1.26.7–12: satiātur ipsa

    Stresses the woman, or the thing named by a feminine noun: ipsa merum sēcum portat, the fig brings its own wine. As with “himself”, ipsa agrees with the subject or the object, whichever is stressed.

Examples

  • tum cornīx plēnā pluviam vocat improba vōce et sōla in siccā sēcum spatiātur harēnā

    Then the shameless crow calls for rain with full voice and struts alone by herself on the dry sand.Verg. G. 1.388–389

  • Chīa senī similis Bacchō, quem Sētia mīsit, ipsa merum sēcum portat et ipsa salem

    Chian figs: like old Bacchus, whom Setia sent, she brings her own neat wine with her, and her own salt.Mart. 13.23.1–2

  • quae vulpem cum revocāsset, intrītō cibō plēnam lagōnam posuit: huic rōstrum īnserēns satiātur ipsa et torquet convīvam famē. quae cum lagōnae collum frūstrā lamberet, peregrīnam sīc locūtam volucrem accēpimus: sua quisque exempla dēbet aequō animō patī

    Inviting the fox in her turn, she set before her a flask full of minced food; thrusting her beak into it, she ate her fill herself and tormented her guest with hunger. When the fox licked the neck of the flask in vain, the bird is said to have spoken thus: “Everyone should bear with good grace the example he has set.”Phaedr. 1.26.7–12

  • amābat enim sēcum praesentiam meam mōre mātrum

    For she loved to have me with her, as mothers do.Aug. Conf. 5.8.15

  • ego ipsa sum, inquit, hīc hospita

    “I’m only a guest here myself,” she said.Cic. Att. 5.1.3

See also she, himself, itself, themselves.
